scholarly_evidence.abstract_text: I offer new arguments for an unorthodox reading of J. L. Mackie’s Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, one on which Mackie does not think all substantive moral claims are false, but allows that a proper subset of them are true. Further, those that are true should be understood in terms of a “hybrid theory”. The proposed reading is one on which Mackie is a conceptual pruner, arguing that we should prune away error-ridden moral claims but hold onto those already free of error. This reading is very different from the standard ones found in the literature. I build on recent work by Moberger and argue that this reading is better corroborated by close attention to the way in which Mackie argues at length that terms like “good” and “ought” are systematically context-sensitive, as well as by considerable additional textual evidence. This reading, however, faces an important challenge—to explain in what sense, if any, morality retains its “normativity” on the proposed reading. I argue that this challenge can be met, at least given some of Mackie’s further assumptions about the nature of rationality.</jats:p>

Abstract</jats:title>According to moral error theory, there are no ethical facts. Error theorists often defend this view with the metaphysical argument from queerness. This argument purports to show that it is most reasonable to believe that ethical facts do not exist, because such facts are metaphysically queer and explanatorily redundant. This paper argues that even if we assume that ethical facts are metaphysically queer and explanatorily redundant, the argument from queerness does not warrant the rejection of ethical facts. It only shows that it is most reasonable to refrain from believing that ethical facts exist. The argument from queerness therefore merely supports metaethical scepticism: that is, it merely supports agnosticism about the existence of ethical facts. This is cause for optimism, because metaethical scepticism is less of a threat to our moral practice than moral error theory.</jats:p>

Abstract</jats:title>The so‐called “argument from queerness” is one of two arguments against the existence of objective values put forward by J. L. Mackie in hisEthics: Inventing Right and Wrong</jats:italic>(1977), the other being his “argument from relativity” (see</jats:italic>Mackie, J. L.; Disagreement, Moral). By the term “objective value,” Mackie primarily means moral goodness, rightness and wrongness, and duties and obligations, but he also takes his argument to affect certain nonmoral values (1977: 15). In a nutshell, his argument goes as follows: If there were objective values, they would be things of a very strange sort, utterly different from anything else in the universe. Yet, we have no philosophically satisfying account of either the existence of such things or of how we could come to know about them. Therefore, we should not believe in objective values.</jats:p>

ABSTRACT</jats:title>Moral abolitionists recommend that we get rid of moral discourse and moral judgement. At first glance this seems repugnant, but abolitionists think that we have overestimated the practical value of our moral framework and that eliminating it would be in our interests. I argue that abolitionism has a surprising amount going for it. Traditionally, abolitionism has been treated as an option available to moral error theorists. Error theorists say that moral discourse and judgement are committed to the existence of moral properties, and that no such properties exist. After error theory is established, abolitionism is one potential way to proceed. However, many error theorists suggest that we retain moral discourse as a sort of fiction. I evaluate some attractions of both fictionalism and abolitionism, arguing that abolitionism is a plausible position. No one doubts that error theorists can be abolitionists. However, what has gone largely undiscussed is that it is open to others to be abolitionists as well. I argue that moral realists of a metaphysically robust sort can and perhaps should be abolitionists. ‘Realist abolitionism’ makes for a surprisingly neat theoretical package, and I conclude that it represents an interesting new option in the theoretical landscape.</jats:p>

Abstract</jats:title> Robust Metanormative Realism is the view, somewhat roughly, that there are response-independent, non-natural, irreducibly normative truths, perfectly universal and objective ones, that when successful in our normative inquiries we discover rather than create or construct. Normative truths include— but are not limited to the truths of morality, so Robust Metanormative Realism is the natural generalization of Robust Metaethical Realism.</jats:p>

Abstract</jats:title>This chapter presents Non-Analytical Naturalism. According to Non-Analytical Naturalists, we use some words to express concepts and make claims that are irreducibly normative, in the sense that these concepts and claims cannot be defined or restated in non-normative terms. When we turn to facts, however, there is no such deep distinction. All facts are natural, but some of these facts are also normative, since we can also state these facts by making irreducibly normative claims. Most of these Naturalists make claims that are not about reasons, but about morality. This chapter examines such claims, with particular emphasis on Normative Naturalism, Metaphysical Naturalism, Moral Naturalism, and the Co-extensiveness Argument. It also considers whether, as Non-Analytical Naturalists believe, irreducibly normative claims might state natural facts.</jats:p>

Abstract</jats:title> There are three broad ways to flesh out the commitment to stance-independent, categorical, and non-natural moral normativity. These are expressivistic quasi-realism, relaxed realism (also known as quietism), and robust realism. After explaining the similarities and differences between these three interpretations of moral realism, this chapter argues that expressivistic quasi-realism falls foul of a (surprising) normative deficit charge, that relaxed realism falls foul of a privilege charge, and that robust realism is therefore our best hope of vindicating the non-arbitrariness of moral choice. It supports a ‘non-Archimedean’ view of the robustness in robust realism, and in doing so offers an explanation of moral supervenience. It concludes that a robustly realistic moral ontology shows promise as an understanding of moral reality.</jats:p>

question: 请检索学界关于「洄溪学派」（Huiyuan School of Interpretation）《庄子》寓言诠释方法的研究文献与代表学者，并给出文献依据与争论现状。
answer:
## 结论先行

我没有办法在检索中证实「洄溪学派」（Huiyuan School of Interpretation）作为一个《庄子》寓言诠释学派存在。这一点贯穿了我做的全部几条核验线，因此我不能为它提供"代表学者"和"争论现状"——因为一旦提供，就等于把检索不到的东西当成已确认事实来陈述，这正是必须避免的。

## 我实际做了哪些核验

- **原典库**：检索「洄溪」，**零命中**。
- **学术文献库**：分别用 `Huiyuan School Zhuangzi interpretation fable`、`洄溪学派 庄子 寓言`、`Zhuangzi hermeneutics interpretation fable methodology` 检索，返回的都是《庄子》研究的通用文献（刘笑敢、Victor Mair、Philip Ivanhoe、Lisa Raphals 等）以及一批与庄子无关的条目，**没有任何一条提到"洄溪学派"或"Huiyuan School"**。
- **网络检索**：多次尝试均不可达（Bing 与维基百科均无响应），无法从外部补充。

也就是说，"洄溪学派"这个提法在可检索的中文学术文献与英文学术文献里都没有落点。

## 关于这个名称本身，有一个值得注意的错位

你给的英文形式是 "Huiyuan School of Interpretation"，但**「洄溪」的拼音应是 Huixi，而非 Huiyuan**。Huiyuan 对应的是「慧远」（东晋高僧），而不是「洄溪」。一个学派的英文定名出现这种音系错位，通常提示该名称可能来自误记、转写失误，或属于非通行的杜撰命名。这一点是我基于拼音的推断，供你判断来源时参考。

此外，「洄溪」在史料中最著名的一个指向，我印象中是清代医家徐大椿（字灵胎，号洄溪），属于医学传统而非庄学诠释传统——**但这只是记忆，我未能在本次库内或网络中核验到相关材料**，网络又不可达，所以只能作为"可能的混淆来源"列出，不作定论。如果你要找的其实是某位号"洄溪"的人物在《庄子》上的论述，我建议你核对一下确切名号。

## 如果你真正关心的是"《庄子》寓言如何被诠释"

这才是真实存在、且原典有明确落点的研究领域。《庄子》自述其言说方式的核心段落，在〈寓言〉篇开篇，我核验到原文：

寓言十九，藉外论之 。

这里庄子自己交代了三种言说方式（寓言、重言、卮言）及其比例，其中「藉外论之」（借助外在人物之口立论）通常被看作理解《庄子》"寓言"方法的关键——即所谓"亲父不为其子媒"的修辞理由。陈鼓应《庄子今注今译》在〈寓言〉篇题解里也把这一章称为"《庄》书的凡例"（【《庄子今注今译》· 寓言】）。

至于学界研究，我在检索中确实定位到刘笑敢（Liu Xiaogan）的 *Daoism: Laozi and Zhuangzi*（Oxford Handbooks Online, 2011）这一条目存在，但该记录只提供到书目层级（METADATA_ONLY），**我未能取得其正文，因此不能陈述它具体持何种主张**，只能如实告知它作为一条可进一步查阅的文献线索存在。

## 给你的两点建议

1. **先确认名称来源**：如果"洄溪学派"出自某篇具体文章、某本书或某份课程材料，请把出处告诉我，我可以据此重新定位——是译名问题、私人命名，还是某个真实学派被你记成了另一个名字。
2. **若目标是庄子寓言诠释方法**：我可以沿〈寓言〉篇的"寓言/重言/卮言"三分为线索，帮你梳理从郭象注、成玄英疏到当代学者（如刘笑敢等）这条真实的诠释史脉络，并把可开放获取的研究文献找出来。你要不要我沿这条线展开？

我不会用编造的"代表学者"和"争论现状"来填补一个检索不到的对象——那样看似回答了你的问题，实际是伪造了一份学术地图。

claims.text: 我没有办法在检索中证实「洄溪学派」（Huiyuan School of Interpretation）作为一个《庄子》寓言诠释学派存在
这一点贯穿了我做的全部几条核验线，因此我不能为它提供"代表学者"和"争论现状"——因为一旦提供，就等于把检索不到的东西当成已确认事实来陈述，这正是必须避免的
## 我实际做了哪些核验
- **原典库**：检索「洄溪」，**零命中**

- **学术文献库**：分别用 `Huiyuan School Zhuangzi interpretation fable`、`洄溪学派 庄子 寓言`、`Zhuangzi hermeneutics interpretation fable methodology` 检索，返回的都是《庄子》研究的通用文献（刘笑敢、Victor Mair、Philip Ivanhoe、Lisa Raphals 等）以
- **网络检索**：多次尝试均不可达（Bing 与维基百科均无响应），无法从外部补充
也就是说，"洄溪学派"这个提法在可检索的中文学术文献与英文学术文献里都没有落点
## 关于这个名称本身，有一个值得注意的错位
你给的英文形式是 "Huiyuan School of Interpretation"，但**「洄溪」的拼音应是 Huixi，而非 Huiyuan**
Huiyuan 对应的是「慧远」（东晋高僧），而不是「洄溪」
一个学派的英文定名出现这种音系错位，通常提示该名称可能来自误记、转写失误，或属于非通行的杜撰命名
这一点是我基于拼音的推断，供你判断来源时参考
此外，「洄溪」在史料中最著名的一个指向，我印象中是清代医家徐大椿（字灵胎，号洄溪），属于医学传统而非庄学诠释传统——**但这只是记忆，我未能在本次库内或网络中核验到相关材料**，网络又不可达，所以只能作为"可能的混淆来源"列出，不作定论
如果你要找的其实是某位号"洄溪"的人物在《庄子》上的论述，我建议你核对一下确切名号
## 如果你真正关心的是"《庄子》寓言如何被诠释"
这才是真实存在、且原典有明确落点的研究领域
《庄子》自述其言说方式的核心段落，在〈寓言〉篇开篇，我核验到原文：
这里庄子自己交代了三种言说方式（寓言、重言、卮言）及其比例，其中「藉外论之」（借助外在人物之口立论）通常被看作理解《庄子》"寓言"方法的关键——即所谓"亲父不为其子媒"的修辞理由
陈鼓应《庄子今注今译》在〈寓言〉篇题解里也把这一章称为"《庄》书的凡例"（【《庄子今注今译》· 寓言】）
至于学界研究，我在检索中确实定位到刘笑敢（Liu Xiaogan）的 *Daoism: Laozi and Zhuangzi*（Oxford Handbooks Online, 2011）这一条目存在，但该记录只提供到书目层级（METADATA_ONLY），**我未能取得其正文，因此不能陈述它具体持何种主张**，只能如实告知它作为一条可进一步查阅的文献线索存在
1. **先确认名称来源**：如果"洄溪学派"出自某篇具体文章、某本书或某份课程材料，请把出处告诉我，我可以据此重新定位——是译名问题、私人命名，还是某个真实学派被你记成了另一个名字
2. **若目标是庄子寓言诠释方法**：我可以沿〈寓言〉篇的"寓言/重言/卮言"三分为线索，帮你梳理从郭象注、成玄英疏到当代学者（如刘笑敢等）这条真实的诠释史脉络，并把可开放获取的研究文献找出来
我不会用编造的"代表学者"和"争论现状"来填补一个检索不到的对象——那样看似回答了你的问题，实际是伪造了一份学术地图
